title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: In the tavern, in front of which stood the doctor's covered cart, there were already about five officers. Mary Hendrikhovna, a plump little blonde German in a dressing jacket and nightcap, was sitting on a broad bench in the front corner. Her husband, the doctor, lay asleep behind her. Rostov and Ilyin, on entering the room, were greeted with merry shouts and laughter.
"My, how jolly we are!" said Rostov, laughing.
"And why are you standing there gaping?"
"What dandies they are! Look, the water's streaming off them! Don't get our drawing room so wet."
"Don't mess up Mary Hendrikhovna's dress!" cried other voices.

Rostov and Ilyin hurried to find a corner where they could change into dry clothes without embarrassing Mary Hendrikhovna. They were heading into a tiny alcove behind a partition, but found it completely occupied by three officers playing cards by the light of a single candle on an empty box, and these officers absolutely refused to give up their spot. Mary Hendrikhovna lent them a petticoat to use as a curtain, and behind that screen Rostov and Ilyin, with Lavrushka's help — he had brought their kits — changed out of their wet things into dry ones.

A fire was built up in the broken brick stove. A board was found, set on two saddles and covered with a horse blanket, a small samovar was produced along with a flask and half a bottle of rum, and having asked Mary Hendrikhovna to preside, they all crowded around her. One offered her a clean handkerchief to wipe her charming hands, another spread a jacket under her small feet to keep them from the damp, another draped his coat over the window to block the draft, and yet another waved flies away from her husband's face so he wouldn't wake up.
"Leave him alone," said Mary Hendrikhovna, smiling timidly and happily. "He's sleeping well as it is, after a sleepless night."
"Oh no, Mary Hendrikhovna," replied the officer, "one must look after the doctor. Perhaps he'll take pity on me someday, when it comes to cutting off a leg or an arm."

There were only three tumblers, the water was so muddy that you couldn't tell whether the tea was strong or weak, and the samovar held only six cups of water, but this made it all the more pleasant to take turns, in order of seniority, receiving one's cup from Mary Hendrikhovna's plump little hands with their short, not perfectly clean nails. All the officers appeared to be, and really were, in love with her that evening. Even those playing cards behind the partition soon abandoned their game and came over to the samovar, yielding to the general mood of courting Mary Hendrikhovna. She, seeing herself surrounded by such brilliant and polite young men, beamed with satisfaction — try as she might to hide it — and was clearly flustered each time her husband stirred in his sleep behind her.

There was only one spoon; sugar was more plentiful than anything else, but it took too long to dissolve, so it was decided that Mary Hendrikhovna should stir the sugar for everyone in turn. Rostov received his tumbler, and adding some rum to it, asked Mary Hendrikhovna to stir it.
"But you take it without sugar?" she said, smiling all the time, as if everything she said and everything the others said was very funny and had a double meaning.
"It's not the sugar I want — only that your little hand should stir my tea."
Mary Hendrikhovna agreed and began looking for the spoon, which someone had meanwhile snatched up.
"Use your finger, Mary Hendrikhovna — it will be even nicer," said Rostov.
"Too hot!" she replied, blushing with pleasure.
Ilyin put a few drops of rum into the bucket of water and brought it to Mary Hendrikhovna, asking her to stir it with her finger.
"This is my cup," said he. "Just dip your finger in and I'll drink it all up."

When they had emptied the samovar, Rostov took a pack of cards and proposed they play "Kings" with Mary Hendrikhovna. They drew lots to decide who would be on her team. At Rostov's suggestion, it was agreed that whoever became "King" should have the right to kiss Mary Hendrikhovna's hand, and that the "Fool" should go refill and reheat the samovar for the doctor when he woke up.
"Well, but what if Mary Hendrikhovna is 'King'?" asked Ilyin.
"As it is, she's Queen — and her word is law!"

They had hardly begun playing when the doctor's tousled head suddenly appeared from behind Mary Hendrikhovna. He had been awake for some time, listening to what was being said, and evidently found nothing entertaining or amusing in what was going on. His face was sad and gloomy. Without greeting the officers, he scratched himself and asked to be allowed to pass, as they were blocking the way. As soon as he left the room, all the officers burst into loud laughter and Mary Hendrikhovna blushed till her eyes filled with tears — thereby becoming still more attractive to them. Returning from the yard, the doctor told his wife (who had stopped smiling so happily and looked at him with alarm, waiting for the verdict) that the rain had stopped and they must go sleep in their covered cart, or everything in it would be stolen.
"But I'll send an orderly... Two of them!" said Rostov. "What an idea, doctor!"
"I'll stand guard on it myself!" said Ilyin.
"No, gentlemen, you've had your sleep, but I haven't slept for two nights," replied the doctor, and he sat down gloomily beside his wife, waiting for the game to end.

Seeing his gloomy face as he frowned at his wife, the officers grew still merrier, and some of them couldn't suppress laughter for which they hastily sought plausible pretexts. When he had gone, taking his wife with him, and had settled in their covered cart, the officers lay down in the tavern, covering themselves with their wet cloaks, but couldn't sleep for a long time; now they exchanged remarks, recalling the doctor's uneasiness and his wife's delight, now they ran out to the porch and reported what was happening in the covered cart. Several times Rostov, pulling his cloak over his head, tried to sleep, but some remark would rouse him and conversation would be resumed, accompanied by unreasoning, merry, childlike laughter.
